title: Canada sees recovery broadening while gasoline explains most of the inflation overshoot
summary: Governing Council held the overnight rate at 2.25% on 15 July. The Bank Rate remained 2.50% and the deposit rate 2.20%. The July projection combined a stronger second quarter, a weak year overall and an inflation overshoot concentrated in gasoline. The Bank estimated second-quarter growth at 2½%, yet projected only 0.7% growth for 2026. Those figures describe a quarter’s pace and a full year’s growth respectively. A rebound after a stalled period can deliver both outcomes. Council considered the existing rate compatible with a gradual absorption of spare capacity and a return of inflation to around 2% in early 2027. The inflation timing depended materially on the path of oil and gasoline prices.

The Bank attributed much of the near-term rebound to the reversal of temporary factors, but also identified signs of improvement across several sources of demand. Consumer spending appeared solid, weak housing activity appeared to be stabilising and exports had resumed growing, albeit on a lower path. Oil and gas investment was expected to support a modest pick-up in business investment. Government spending contributed across the projection. Businesses increasingly reported learning how to operate amid uncertainty even as the Canada–US–Mexico Agreement became subject to annual reviews. Adaptation could raise exports from depressed levels without fully reversing the loss of output relative to an earlier path. An increase in quarterly exports and persistent damage from tariffs can therefore coexist.

The labour market remained the clearest reservation. Unemployment stood at 6.5% in June and had stayed within a 6½%–7% range since late 2024. Council saw economic slack despite the faster quarterly GDP estimate. It forecast Canadian GDP growth of 1.8% in each of 2027 and 2028, with that slack closing gradually as the recovery continued. Slower population growth also affected the interpretation of the aggregate data. Distinguishing growth in total spending from growth per person would help establish how much momentum individual households were contributing. The press release provides neither a numerical output-gap estimate nor a projected quarter in which capacity would be fully utilised.

May headline CPI was 3.2%, compared with 2.2% excluding gasoline, while underlying measures remained close to 2%. The difference between the two annual growth rates illustrates how sensitive the headline was to fuel. It is not an exact percentage-point contribution from gasoline because excluding a component changes the weights applied to the remaining basket. The Bank saw war-related costs entering some other prices but also saw spare capacity restraining prices elsewhere. Short-horizon inflation expectations were sensitive to gasoline, whereas longer-term expectations remained anchored. A rise in the near-term survey response could therefore be consistent with the Bank’s projected return to target. What would challenge the outlook was broader persistent pass-through, a prolonged energy shock or changes in expectations beyond the near term.

International demand and financing offered offsetting influences. The Bank projected world growth of about 2¾% in 2026 and roughly 3¼% in the next two years, as the Middle East conflict weighed against the expansion in AI investment. Canadian financial conditions had eased since April. US bond yields had risen while Canadian yields were little changed, and the Bank judged this interest-rate differential had contributed to depreciation of the Canadian dollar. That comparison concerns market yields and an exchange-rate movement over preceding months. The statement supplies no probability that investors had assigned to the July decision or observed announcement-window returns. The policy signal was Council’s assessment that the rate could support the recovery while underlying inflation stayed near target; the yield and currency observations provide context for testing how investors received that assessment.

questions.question: How much of the second-quarter rebound will persist after temporary factors reverse?
questions.detail: Compare the July estimate with subsequent GDP releases by expenditure, separately tracking final sales, inventories, exports and investment outside oil and gas. Pair these with hours and household spending per person. This would test whether the rebound marks a sustained narrowing of slack or a return to normal production after temporary disruptions.

questions.question: How exposed is the projected return to 2% to a slower decline in gasoline prices?
questions.detail: Construct alternative fuel paths with the same non-fuel basket, allowing for annual base effects, then compare observed services and goods inflation with those benchmarks. Track near- and longer-horizon expectations separately. A delay in the headline return caused by fuel alone would have different implications from an equal delay accompanied by broader repricing.

questions.question: What part of the weaker Canadian dollar reflected the US–Canada yield differential?
questions.detail: Compare matched-maturity yield spreads, oil prices, broad US-dollar moves and the bilateral exchange rate across the interval the Bank describes. Then examine the announcement in a separate, shorter window. This would distinguish a global rise in US yields from a reassessment of the Canadian outlook and help quantify the import-cost channel. Use quotes from matching hours, since a Canadian close compared with an earlier US observation could exaggerate the apparent divergence.
